idiom_name: model_dump(mode='json', include=fields) backed by a validated field set
implementation_notes: Pydantic takes the caller's field set directly: model_dump/model_dump_json accept include/exclude as a set of field names or a nested dictionary for sub-selections, and the model knows its own vocabulary via model_fields. The boundary maps the fields query parameter onto that set, validates it, and lets the serializer do the projection - which is what FastAPI response models build on. The classic hand-written DTO layer is replaced by one argument.
pitfalls: include/exclude silently ignore names the model does not have, so the explicit model_fields check is what turns a typo into a 400 instead of a smaller payload.
Scalar True versus a nested set inside include ({'user': {'id'}}) have different meanings for sub-models; getting it wrong either drops the whole sub-object or leaks all of it.
model_dump() to a dict and then json.dumps doubles the work - use model_dump_json when the reply goes straight to the wire.
Pydantic v1 spells this .dict(include=...) / .json(include=...); a mixed-version codebase silently loses the projection.

variants.name: stdlib dataclasses projection
variants.implementation_notes: When the service has no serialization framework, dataclasses.fields gives the vocabulary and asdict gives the values, so the projection is a dict comprehension over the requested names with an explicit unknown-field error. Zero dependencies and obviously correct; the price is that validation, aliasing and camelCase conversion stay hand-written, and the projection happens after the nested structure has been materialized.
pitfalls: asdict is recursive and deep-copies every value before the filter runs, so the compute saving is zero - only bytes shrink.
API/alias names (camelCase, reserved words) are not derived from the dataclass, so a public field vocabulary needs its own mapping table.
Nested dataclasses/lists are not filtered at all: the whole nested value is copied unless the helper recurses explicitly.
